knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Checking for frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges, and confirming the tool suits the surface and hygiene zone, is correct. The procedure says to select tools for soil, finish and hygiene zone and to check frayed fibres, damaged handles and sharp edges. Using a toilet-area tool in the kitchen crosses hygiene zones, so it is not a valid check.
Tools are segregated by zone and a tool from a contaminated zone is replaced with the site-assigned clean tool.
The worked scenario removes the toilet-area brush and replaces it with the site-assigned clean tool, which the lesson requires for cross-contamination control.

A brush from the toilet area used in the kitchen kit is the unsafe alternative, because it carries contamination from one hygiene zone into another. The other options are approved practice: a kitchen-dedicated cloth, a separate tool for the reception area, and a squeegee checked for damaged edges.

Removing the damaged tool from use and reporting it so it can be replaced is the correct record or escalation. Damaged or cross-contaminated tools are taken out of use, segregated and recorded for reprocessing or replacement. Continuing to use a damaged tool or keeping a note only on your phone does not meet this.

practicalCriteria: Protects finishes, hands and hygiene boundaries.
Explains applicable scope and site procedures
Demonstrates hazard controls and safe stop-work decisions
passRule: 80% on knowledge checks; practical sign-off separate
evidenceRequired: Assessor observation record covering procedure steps 1-7
stopWorkCriteria: Stop work if procedure step 6 is not done: Before acting, ask what the surface is, what the soil or hazard is, which product or method is approved, and what could harm a person, property or food.
Stop work if procedure step 7 is not done: If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.
